thread.title: Best Buy: The Best Buy In Retail Right Now - Best Buy Co. (NYSE:BBY)

author: Jeff Vande Hey
title: Best Buy: The Best Buy In Retail Right Now - Best Buy Co. (NYSE:BBY)
text:
With a slowing housing market, global growth concerns and continuing trade tensions between the world's two largest economies, we have a market that seems afraid to go up. In fact, as shown below, the overall market has dropped by over 10% in the past three months. In such an environment, investors have to decide whether they will sit tight while the carnage continues or go bargain hunting and find individual cases where declines might be overdone. In this article, we take a look at Best Buy ( BBY ) to determine if it may fall into the latter category, hence providing a bargain for opportune investors.
Personally, I have had my eye on Best Buy for a while but I just couldn't pull the trigger as the valuation was high enough that I just couldn't convince myself there was a substantial upside. However, with Best Buy stock declining approximately three times the rate of the overall market in the last three months, I have convinced myself that the market has provided us with an attractive entry point. The reasons for my investing thesis will be laid out below.
BBY data by YCharts
Competitive Environment While a case could be made that Best Buy is in a niche all its own and it has no highly similar peers, there is no doubt that each segment of its business has plenty of competition. Fry's Electronics may be its most similar competitor in the big box arena and while its sales can't approach Best Buy's 2017 revenue of $39.4 billion, Fry's 2.4 billion is nothing to sneeze at. Apple Store, Microsoft Store, Walmart,( WMT ) and Target ( TGT ) also provide competition in certain segments of Best Buy's brick and mortar operations. Best Buy's online business, which accounted for 20% of all revenue in Q4, faces significant competition from Amazon ( AMZN ) and also faces competition from Newegg and Tiger Direct, among others.
Frenemies As often happens in business, there is a fuzzy line between Best Buy's friends and enemies. In Best Buy's case, frenemies include Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft,( MSFT ) both of which compete with Best Buy in bricks and mortar sales but also have partnerships where they utilize Best Buy to get their products sold. This has worked out well for Best Buy and there have been several reports that Best Buy sells approximately as many Apple products as Apple Stores. While it is a stretch to say Apple needs Best Buy as much as Best Buy needs Apple, they definitely both help each other. Interestingly, Business Insider recently did an Apple Store vs. Best Buy investigative comparison with Best Buy coming out as the clear winner.
IMAGE SOURCE: BEST BUY
Cheaper Than You Think By common investing metrics, the recent pullback has resulted in a valuation that is not only attractive from a historical standpoint, but it is also cheap relative to competitors. Best Buy currently sports a PEG ratio of .66 and an Enterprise Value/Ebitda ratio of 5.51. Those ratios are low by almost any standards. In addition, the reported PE of 14 might actually be a little high. A closer look shows the last four quarters of earnings coming in at $5.08 (2.42+.82+.91+.93) . Those numbers, when combined with the current share price of $55.37, provide a trailing 12 month PE of 10.89.
Company PEG Enterprise Value/EBITDA Best Buy .66 5.51 Walmart 4.61 10.05 Target 1.55 7.10 Microsoft N/A 16.67 Apple .99 10.51 DATA SOURCES: THOMSON REUTERS AND CAPITAL IQ
Catalysts and Caution Flags A bear or bull case can be made for almost any stock. If that weren't true, we would all be rich. With regard to Best Buy, one caution flag is the fact that the general market pullback could continue indefinitely. If you are bearish on the market, you may want to wait for an even better entry point. Another yield sign may be the fact that Amazon is a significant competitor. With Jeff Bezos' catchphrase being "Your margin is my opportunity", we know that Amazon doesn't really care about high margins and is willing to trade sales volume for margin, which can compress margins for competitors as well. In addition, the holiday season is here and while that is generally a catalyst, we know that holiday deals and deep discounts are rampant and if discounting becomes too deep, profits take a hit.
On the plus side, we have to tip our hat to management. CEO Hubert Joly has engineered an impressive turnaround since he took the reins six years ago and has shown both a willingness to adapt and the ability to succeed in a highly competitive environment.
In the four years before Joly took over, Best Buy's revenue was flat, earnings were declining and the stock price was more than halved. Since that time, earnings have risen rapidly, margins have more than tripled and the stock price is up 113%. Best Buy has accomplished these things by cutting expenses while building out its online business and as importantly, emphasizing customer service .
BBY data by YCharts
Final Take For a value investor, it is all about price. While I have been impressed with management's execution for some time now, it is only after the recent price drop that I have seriously considered investing in Best Buy stock. Best Buy is a best in breed stock and with a couple generations of gamers coming up, I don't expect the demand for consumer electronics to decline any time soon. While I am not sure where the overall market is going in the near future, I do think the decline is overdone. The fact that Best Buy pays a 3% dividend and has beaten estimates in each of the last four quarters is just icing on the cake. While I haven't pulled the trigger yet, it is very possible I will be a Best Buy shareholder before the holidays hit. If you are a value investor, I would encourage you to do your own due diligence and give this retail stock a close look.
